opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a bit of a provocative phrase, I admit. What I mean is this. If you look at how large language models became so powerful, the core reason is that we essentially "downloaded" a huge part of human knowledge from the internet. All the text people have written over centuries, compressed into a model. In a sense, we've already downloaded humanity once, but only through one very narrow channel: language.

Language is incredibly powerful, but it's also a very lossy projection of what humans actually are. When you write something down, you've already done a lot of abstraction. All the perception, the intuition, the physical interaction with the world that led you to that sentence is gone. A child learns an enormous amount about objects, space, causality, and other people long before they can say anything about it. None of that is really in the text corpus.

So when I say "downloading humans" as a direction for data, I mean asking: how do we capture the rest of it? How do we get data that reflects how humans see, move, act, and make decisions in the real world, not just what they eventually wrote about it? That could mean egocentric video, recordings of people doing tasks, sensory and embodied signals, data that captures the process and not just the final output.

I also think this matters because the text well is running dry. We've more or less used up the high-quality internet text. If we want the next leap, especially toward models that actually understand the physical world, what people call world models or spatial intelligence, we need a new source of data that's equally rich. And the richest source we know of is human experience itself.

Of course, there are lots of hard questions. How do you collect this at scale? How do you do it respecting privacy? What's the right representation, because raw pixels and sensor streams aren't the same as tokens. But as a direction, I think it's where things have to go. The first wave was downloading what humans said. The next wave is, in some sense, downloading how humans experience and interact with the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The phrase comes from thinking about where the next big source of training signal is going to come from. Language models got as far as they did because the internet is, in a sense, a giant compressed record of human thought. People wrote down what they know, how they reason, what they argue about. Text is a very lossy but very dense compression of human knowledge, and we just scraped all of it.

For vision and for embodied intelligence, we don't have that. Images and videos on the internet are not a record of how humans perceive or act in the world. They're a record of what humans decided to photograph and upload, which is a very biased, very passive slice. A model watching YouTube learns what the world looks like from a camera someone pointed at something interesting. It doesn't learn what it's like to walk into a kitchen, decide what to do, look around, pick something up, make a mistake, correct it.

So when I say "downloading humans," I mean something like this: instead of only scraping the artifacts humans left behind, we should be capturing the process itself. What are people looking at, moment to moment? Where does their attention go? What do they do with their hands? What decisions do they make and in what order? That's the actual data of intelligence operating in the physical world, and almost none of it has ever been recorded.

Egocentric video is one piece of this. If you have a lot of people wearing cameras while they go about their lives, you start getting a first-person stream that's much closer to what a robot or an agent would need to learn from. But I think about it more broadly than just video. Gaze, hand motion, speech, the choices people make, the things they ignore. A rich multimodal recording of human behavior at scale.

There's a scale argument here too. The reason the LLM recipe worked is that the data was already there, essentially for free, because billions of people spent decades producing it. Robotics doesn't have that. Teleoperation data is expensive. Simulation has a reality gap. But there are eight billion humans who are already very good at acting in the world, every day, all the time. If you can capture even a small fraction of that, you have a dataset that's orders of magnitude larger than anything you could collect with robots directly.

And the goal isn't to build a copy of a specific person. It's that the aggregate of human behavior contains the priors we actually want: physical common sense, how objects behave, what's worth paying attention to, how to decompose a task. Right now models mostly learn those priors indirectly, through text describing them. I'd rather they learn them from the source.

Of course there are real issues. Privacy is the obvious one, and I don't think we should be casual about it. Consent, what gets recorded, who owns it. Those have to be designed in from the start, not patched later. But I think the direction is right. The frontier of AI data is shifting from what humans wrote down to how humans actually live, and the field that figures out how to capture that responsibly is going to define the next phase.

astra-6.text:
By “downloading humans,” I mean trying to capture the knowledge and judgment that are still inside people’s heads. A lot of AI training has relied on what people have already put on the internet—text, images, code. But that’s only a slice of what we know. An expert might recognize that something is wrong without ever having written down how they recognize it.

So the question becomes: can we create interactions where that expertise becomes training data? Give someone a problem, observe what they do, ask them to compare alternatives or correct a model. You’re trying to capture not just the final answer, but the decisions that lead to it.

“Downloading” is a provocative metaphor. It doesn’t mean copying a person’s consciousness. It means finding ways to turn human knowledge that hasn’t been recorded yet into something a model can learn from.

sol-6.1.text:
By “downloading humans,” I mean trying to capture the knowledge and judgment people have that never makes it onto the internet. A lot of what we know is implicit: how we approach a problem, what we pay attention to, how we recognize that something has gone wrong. The final answer or finished product only reveals a small part of that.

So the question is: can we create interactions where people demonstrate those things, and turn that process into useful training data? Instead of only collecting what humans have already written, you collect how they work, how they make decisions, and how they correct mistakes.

“Downloading” is a metaphor, of course. You’re not copying somebody’s mind. You’re trying to make more of their experience available for a model to learn from. And the difficult part is figuring out what to capture—because recording everything someone does doesn’t automatically tell you why they did it.
